situation:
You and your teammate are the marketing director and the customer experience manager at MERIDIAN MOVING & STORAGE, a regional moving and storage company. The chief executive officer (judge) has asked the two of you to meet about the campaign the company has committed to run for the spring relocation season, when most of the year's household and corporate moves are booked.

Eight months ago MERIDIAN acquired CROSSPOINT VAN LINES, and the two operations have not become one company yet. Crews still work from separate dispatch systems, separate packing standards, and separate incentive pay. The former CROSSPOINT crews arrived with an unusually clean handling record and a documented claims rate under one percent. The legacy MERIDIAN fleet is three times larger, and its crews have never measured damage the same way.

The campaign an outside agency has built rests on a single promise: that a customer's belongings arrive undamaged, guaranteed. The record behind it comes from CROSSPOINT files alone. Making it true fleet-wide would take a company-wide handling and scanning system, retraining every crew to one packing standard, and a claims desk staffed through the season, funded out of next year's operating budget.

That spending is affordable only if a forecast holds. Corporate relocation contracts in the region are projected to grow sharply as two large employers expand, and the campaign is designed to capture that demand. If the expansions slip a year, MERIDIAN carries the system, the retraining, and the claims desk against ordinary residential volume, and the guarantee becomes a promise the company is paying to keep.

The other course is to advertise only what the records support, naming the CROSSPOINT standard as the standard, and let the rest of the fleet earn its way in. That costs little and is fully documented, but it markets half of a company that has spent eight months telling customers and crews it is one company, and leaves the season's positioning to competitors already promising more.

The chief executive officer (judge) wants your recommendation on which promise MERIDIAN will make this spring, what evidence it rests on, and how the crews on both sides of the merger will hear it. You will present in the CEO's office. The CEO (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas. After your presentation and questions, the CEO (judge) will thank you for your work.
